5404               	;
5405               	; 	' ======================================================================
5406               	; 	' DRAWING THE STORE -- four blits, once per screen crossing
5407               	; 	' ======================================================================
5408               	; 	' This is the whole cost of the flip, and it is paid on a discrete event
5409               	; 	' rather than every frame. RallyX's pan repaints 576 chars every time the
5410               	; 	' camera moves one cell; this repaints 640 about once every two seconds
5411               	; 	' of running.
5412               	; 	' SPRITES OFF BEFORE THE BLIT, NOT AFTER IT. This routine WAITs between
5413               	; 	' bands -- one band a frame, because a burst of VDP writes past a few
5414               	; 	' dozen in one frame is silently dropped -- so painting the new screen
5415               	; 	' takes several frames, and for all of them the OLD screen's actors and
5416               	; 	' obstacles were still sitting on top of it. Following Harry through a
5417               	; 	' seam showed him and every cart from the floor he had just left,
5418               	; 	' standing on a shop that was assembling itself underneath them.
5419               	; 	'
5420               	; 	' They are put back by the normal draw on the same pass, so the crossing
5421               	; 	' reads as a cut rather than as a dissolve with ghosts in it.
5422               	; 	' EACH BAND IS FINISHED BEFORE THE FRAME IT IS DRAWN IN ENDS, and the
5423               	; 	' bands go TOP DOWN. Both halves of that matter.
5424               	; 	'
5425               	; 	' The blit paints the template -- shelves, pillars and all -- and the
5426               	; 	' radios and prizes then take out the fixtures they stand in. Those two
5427               	; 	' used to be four frames apart: all four bands blitted with a WAIT
5428               	; 	' between them, and only afterwards the clearing. So every screen change
5429               	; 	' showed its counters and beams for several frames and then erased them,
5430               	; 	' which reads as the shop flickering rather than as it being drawn.
5431               	; 	'
5432               	; 	' TOP DOWN because a band's beam tops are stamped into the SLAB ROW OF
5433               	; 	' THE BAND ABOVE. Going bottom-up, band 1's blit would paint over the
5434               	; 	' beam tops band 0 had just put there. Going top-down the band above is
5435               	; 	' always already drawn, so everything a band needs -- its own cells and
5436               	; 	' the row it borrows overhead -- is final by the time its WAIT arrives.
5437               	; 	'
5438               	; 	' `3 - dq` rather than `FOR dlv = 3 TO 0 STEP -1`: dlv is an unsigned
5439               	; 	' byte, so counting down past zero wraps to 255 and the loop never ends
5440               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A).
5441               	; draw_screen:
5442               cvb_DRAW_SCREEN

5587               	;
5588               	; 	' A SUPPORT BEAM HAS TO REACH THE FLOOR IT HOLDS UP, AND THAT FLOOR IS
5589               	; 	' NOT IN ITS OWN BAND. A beam fills its band's four air rows, so its top
5590               	; 	' pixel sits under the slab row of the band ABOVE -- and a slab row is
5591               	; 	' five pixels of bar over three of green (see SLAB), so the beam stopped
5592               	; 	' three pixels short of the bar on every storey. It read as a beam that
5593               	; 	' misses the floor, which is exactly what it was.
5594               	; 	'
5595               	; 	' It cannot be drawn into either template. The beam belongs to the band
5596               	; 	' below and the row belongs to the band above, and the two templates are
5597               	; 	' chosen independently per screen, so no template knows both. So the
5598               	; 	' band blits go down first and the tops are stamped afterwards, from a
5599               	; 	' per-template column table -- the same shape as the escalator's head cap.
5600               	; 	'
5601               	; 	' Bands 0 and 1 only. Band 2's top row is the ROOF DECK, which is grey
5602               	; 	' over grey with no green to bridge, and the roof itself has no band
5603               	; 	' above it at all.
5604               	; 	' BANDS 0 TO 2 -- ALL THREE SHOPPING FLOORS. It used to stop at 1,
5605               	; 	' because band 2's ceiling is the ROOF DECK and the deck had no green
5606               	; 	' under it: a beam there already ran straight into grey and needed
5607               	; 	' nothing. Giving the roof its three green rows (so the lift shaft stops
5608               	; 	' under it, like every other floor) took that away, and the top floor's
5609               	; 	' beams started falling three pixels short.
5610               	; 	'
5611               	; 	' So the roof gets its own version of the stamp. A beam HOLDS THE ROOF

6388               	; 			' THE BALL IS ON THE GROUND WHEN HE GETS TO IT.
6389               	; 			'
6390               	; 			' The bounce phase used to be `lx AND 31` -- a byte out of
6391               	; 			' the placement table, which is to say arbitrary. Run onto
6392               	; 			' a screen and the first ball might be at the bottom of its
6393               	; 			' arc, where a jump clears it, or at the top, where it has
6394               	; 			' to be ducked, and nothing on the way in told you which.
6395               	; 			' Sometimes you could keep running and jump it; sometimes

6400               	; 			' closes 4 px a pass and the ball 2, so they meet in

6402               	; 			' at 32, so seeding it with the NEGATIVE of that lands it on
6403               	; 			' phase 0 -- the ground -- exactly as they arrive.

6602               	; 		' ------------------------------------------- the THIRD radio
6603               	; 		' Past the two table slots the band has one more, at 8+llv, and
6604               	; 		' it is A RADIO OR NOTHING. Its kind does NOT come from the
6605               	; 		' table: the two bytes for slot 2 are still there and still
6606               	; 		' skipped, so the six-byte stride and every placement in
6607               	; 		' store.bas are untouched.
6608               	; 		'
6609               	; 		' It is synthesised from the band's own slot 0 instead -- a
6610               	; 		' third radio appears only where that band already has radios,
6611               	; 		' which is what "a floor carries one, two or three of them"
6612               	; 		' means. Reading a kind out of the table here would have let a
6613               	; 		' third BALL through, and a third ball is a fifth sprite on the
6614               	; 		' scanline, the one thing the two-slot cap exists to prevent.
6615               	; 		'
6616               	; 		' Krook 8, measured: assets/ref2600/hazards.md counts the
6617               	; 		' original's radios at three fixed positions and finds the third
6618               	; 		' arriving two rounds after the second.
6619               	; 		'
6620               	; 		' ONLY THE FIELDS THAT ARE EVER READ BACK are written. obd, obh,
6621               	; 		' obp and obc are write-only at 8-11 -- draw_obst and the
6622               	; 		' obstacle update both stop at 7, and coll_obst reads obh only
6623               	; 		' for a BALL, which this slot can never hold. obht IS read: it
6624               	; 		' is the hit refractory, and a stale one carried across a screen

7677               	; 	' THE END WALLS ARE MOVEMENT LIMITS, NOT A CLAMP APPLIED AFTERWARDS.

7680               	; 	' walked on to x = 254, the crossing routine then noticed there was no
7681               	; 	' screen 8 and set him to 232 -- a 22 px snap BACKWARDS. He reached the
7682               	; 	' wall and was thrown off it. Testing the limit BEFORE the step means he
7683               	; 	' arrives at the wall and stays there, which is what a wall does.
7684               	; 	' IN THE AIR HE IS BALLISTIC. The horizontal direction is fixed at
7685               	; 	' take-off and the stick is ignored until he lands: steering in mid-air
7686               	; 	' is not a jump, it is flight, and it also let him flip which way he was
7687               	; 	' facing halfway through an arc. kjdx is 0 for a standing jump, 1 for a
7688               	; 	' running one to the right, 2 to the left.

8853               	; 	' the screens that carry hazards". That stopped being true the moment
8854               	; 	' hazard placement moved into the per-Krook stor_lvl table, and nothing
8855               	; 	' noticed, because the prize table is not part of the level table and
8856               	; 	' every check was written about one object at a time. Two money bags ended
8857               	; 	' up standing on a radio -- not fighting it, since the two routines poke
8858               	; 	' different cells and the later writer simply wins, so they read as one
8859               	; 	' merged object.
8860               	; 	'
8861               	; 	' WHAT KEEPS THEM APART IS COLUMNS. A radio stands at column 7, 15 or 23
8862               	; 	' (see lrc below); genstore's _off_the_rack nudges a prize clear of all
8863               	; 	' three, and checklevels.py reads that arithmetic back out of THIS file
8864               	; 	' and fails the build on any overlap.
8865               	; 	'
8866               	; 	' rdall = 1 paints all four cells, 0 repaints only the top-right one --
8867               	; 	' the pulse. Same address arithmetic either way, so the two cannot drift.
8868               	; 	' A BEAM TOP HANGS OUT OF THE FLOOR ABOVE, and the beam it belongs to has
8869               	; 	' just been taken away. `beam_tops` stamps SLABP -- the floor bar with the
8870               	; 	' support carried up through its lower three pixel rows -- into the slab
8871               	; 	' row above every pillar, and it runs BEFORE the radios and prizes are
8872               	; 	' placed. Clearing a pillar's own cells therefore left three grey pixels
8873               	; 	' dangling from the ceiling with nothing under them.
8874               	; 	'
8875               	; 	' TESTED, NOT ASSUMED: only SLABP is put back to SLAB. The row above the
8876               	; 	' top shopping floor is the ROOF DECK, a different character altogether,
8877               	; 	' and writing a floor bar over it would punch a hole in the roof.
8878               	; 	' A SHELF RUN IS FIVE CELLS WIDE and a radio covers two, so one standing
8879               	; 	' on a counter punched a hole through its middle and left the ends either
8880               	; 	' side -- the same incoherence the dangling pillar had, and worse, because
8881               	; 	' a counter reads as one object. The whole unit goes: walk outward along
8882               	; 	' the band's row 2 while the cell is still a shelf top, clearing it and
8883               	; 	' its bottom half together.
8884               	; 	'
8885               	; 	' Bounded at eight steps. The runs are five, so eight is slack rather
8886               	; 	' than a guess -- and an unbounded walk would run off the end of the row
8887               	; 	' if the name table ever held something unexpected.
8888               	; 	#if NES
8889               	; 	' WHAT THE TEMPLATE PUT IN THIS CELL, for a target that cannot read its
8890               	; 	' own video memory back. #nta is the offset INSIDE the band (0-159) and
8891               	; 	' nbl is the band; the answer is the byte SCREEN blitted there.
8892               	; 	'
8893               	; 	' This is the same arithmetic the blit itself does in draw_band --
8894               	; 	' template id out of stor_ix for (band, screen), times 160, plus the
8895               	; 	' offset -- so the two cannot disagree about what is on screen. It is
8896               	; 	' reading what the cell MEANS, not guessing from where the cell is: a
8897               	; 	' coordinate is a fact about this layout, the character is a fact about
8898               	; 	' the world, and only the second is safe to erase on.
8899               	; 	' SIXTEEN PATTERNS INTO THE BORROWED SLOTS, ONE VBLANK EACH.
8900               	; 	'
8901               	; 	' This is what esc_stand and esc_run cost on this machine. Four sprites is
8902               	; 	' 16 patterns and **a tile here is SIXTEEN bytes** -- two bitplanes -- so
8903               	; 	' the swap is 256 bytes. Three ways to spend that, and only one works:
8904               	; 	'
8905               	; 	'   nes_def         rendering off, ~2 frames of DARK SCREEN every mount.
8906               	; 	'                   This is the flash that was reported for three sessions.
8907               	; 	'   resident art    no upload at all -- but it needs 16 free patterns per
8908               	; 	'                   facing and there are only twelve free in the whole
8909               	; 	'                   table. Tried, and it overwrote Harry's left-facing legs.
8910               	; 	'   queued, chunked <- this. 64 bytes a vblank, four vblanks, picture up
8911               	; 	'                   the whole time.
8912               	; 	'
8913               	; 	' FOUR CHUNKS BECAUSE ONE WILL NOT FIT. The NMI's copy loop runs to the end
8914               	; 	' of its descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and the PPUADDR/PPUSCROLL
8915               	; 	' restore that follows it re-points the PPU mid-frame if it runs late --
8916               	; 	' which is the whole picture jumping for a frame. About 1679 cycles are
8917               	; 	' available after OAM DMA and a copy costs 50 + 14 a byte, so 64 bytes
8918               	; 	' (946) is comfortable and 256 (3634) is not. The WAITs are load-bearing:
8919               	; 	' PPUBUF accumulates for a whole pass, so without them all four descriptors
8920               	; 	' would flush in one vblank and cost exactly what the single call did.
8921               	; 	' checkvblank.py sums the descriptors BETWEEN WAITs for this reason.
8922               	; 	'
8923               	; 	' The cost is four frames at a mount or a dismount, once each, against two
8924               	; 	' frames of black. The caller sets #nsrc; nes_chrinit copies nchr, ncnt,
8925               	; 	' #ncol and nink into zero page rather than consuming the variables, so
8926               	; 	' they only need setting once.
8927               	; 	'
8928               	; 	' THE INTERMEDIATE STATE IS VISIBLE and that is accepted: for a frame or
8929               	; 	' two Harry is part standing and part running. He is stepping onto a
8930               	; 	' staircase at the time, which is exactly when a limb changing shape reads
8931               	; 	' as him changing pose.
8932               	; nes_swp16:
8933               	; 	' HARRY COMES OFF THE SCREEN FIRST, because this takes four frames.
8934               	; 	'
8935               	; 	' The swap is 256 bytes and a vblank carries about a hundred, so it goes as
8936               	; 	' four queued chunks with a WAIT between them (see below). The game loop is
8937               	; 	' stopped for those frames but the PPU is not, so whatever is half-written
8938               	; 	' is on screen: for a frame or two Harry was part standing and part
8939               	; 	' running -- reported as a glitch when he steps off a flight, and it is
8940               	; 	' one. All four of his sprites differ between the two poses, so there is no
8941               	; 	' ordering of the chunks that stays coherent.
8942               	; 	'
8943               	; 	' He is hidden instead. Four frames of absence at the exact moment he steps
8944               	; 	' on or off a staircase reads as nothing at all, where a figure assembled
8945               	; 	' out of two poses reads as a fault. draw_actors puts him back on its next
8946               	; 	' pass -- no flag to clear, because it writes all four slots every time.
8947               	; 	'
8948               	; 	' AND THE OAM MIRRORS WITH HIM. nes_oam2 copies slots 0-27 into 28-55 to
8949               	; 	' make each 16x16 actor two NES sprites, and it only runs at the end of
8950               	; 	' draw_actors -- which is not running during these WAITs. Without the call
8951               	; 	' below his left half would vanish and his RIGHT half would stay, which is
8952               	; 	' a worse artefact than the one being fixed.
8953               	; 	SPRITE 4,SPRHID,0,0,0
8954               	; 	SPRITE 5,SPRHID,0,0,0
8955               	; 	SPRITE 6,SPRHID,0,0,0
8956               	; 	SPRITE 7,SPRHID,0,0,0
8957               	; 	ASM JSR nes_oam2
8958               	; 	ASM JSR nes_suitcases
8959               	; 	nchr = P_HSTB
8960               	; 	ntab = 0
8961               	; 	#ncol = 0
8962               	; 	nink = 1
8963               	; 	ncnt = 4
8964               	; 	WAIT
8965               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
8966               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32		' four patterns of source art, 8 bytes each
8967               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
8968               	; 	WAIT
8969               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
8970               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32

8974               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32

8984               	;
8985               	; nes_def:
8986               	; 	' WHAT DEFINE WOULD HAVE DONE. CVBasic implements no DEFINE at all for the
8987               	; 	' NES, on the reading that patterns live in cartridge CHR ROM -- but an
8988               	; 	' iNES header with a CHR-bank count of ZERO asks for 8 KB of CHR-RAM
8989               	; 	' instead, and that is the header CVBasic emits whenever the program uses
8990               	; 	' no BITMAP/CHRROM statement. So the pattern table here is ordinary VRAM
8991               	; 	' and this is the write. assets/nes_chr.asm carries the routine and the
8992               	; 	' reasoning; the caller sets #nsrc, nchr, ncnt and ntab.
8993               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrup
8994               	; 	RETURN
8995               	;
8996               	; 	' AND THE SAME THING WITHOUT LOSING A FRAME. nes_def turns rendering off
8997               	; 	' and waits for a vblank the NMI therefore never services, so the game's
8998               	; 	' own WAIT then waits for the one after -- about two frames a call. That
8999               	; 	' is free at setup and ruinous anywhere that runs repeatedly. It builds
9000               	; 	' the same bytes into `nesb` and hands the NMI a single copy descriptor

9008               	; 	' flashing title screen.
9009               	; 	'
9010               	; 	' #nesb must point at a buffer of at least ncnt*16 bytes and is set once
9011               	; 	' in init_tables, which runs before boot: and therefore before the title.

9820               	; 	' THE BOUNCE PHASE, ON THE SAME CLOCK AS THE JUMP AND AT ITS OLD PERIOD.
9821               	; 	'
9822               	; 	' The jump has always advanced by the frame delta (`kjf = kjf + fdv`) while
9823               	; 	' the bounce advanced once per PASS -- so whether a jump cleared a ball
9824               	; 	' depended on how busy the screen was, and the frame-by-frame property
9825               	; 	' checkball.py proves was exact only at fdv = 1.
9826               	; 	'
9827               	; 	' Stepping the phase by fdv directly would fix the clock and wreck the
9828               	; 	' game: a 32-phase arc would drop from about 1.35 s to 0.55 s, balls
9829               	; 	' bouncing 2.4x faster everywhere. So it gets a fraction of its own --
9830               	; 	' 25/64 of a phase per frame is 23.4 phases a second, against the 23.8 it
9831               	; 	' runs at today. Same bounce, now the same clock as the thing that has to
9832               	; 	' clear it.

10097               	;
10098               	; 	' ONE STEP OF A FRACTIONAL SPEED, FOR WHOEVER IS MOVING.
10099               	; 	'
10100               	; 	' `pacc` in and out, `psp64` in (sixty-fourths of a pixel per FRAME),
10101               	; 	' `pspd` out (whole pixels this pass). CVBasic has no locals, so the caller
10102               	; 	' stages its own accumulator in and takes it back out; that costs four
10103               	; 	' statements against the fourteen this used to be, written out per actor.
10104               	; 	'
10105               	; 	' Harry had the only copy. Kelly, the hazards and the bounce phase all need
10106               	; 	' the same thing -- everything the round clock judges has to advance by
10107               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAMES, or the loop rate becomes a difficulty dial and where the
10108               	; 	' player stands decides the outcome (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10109               	; 	'
10110               	; 	' Three drains support up to 192/64 units per frame. The remainder
10111               	; 	' is below 64, so the byte addition cannot exceed 255. Planes use
10112               	; 	' two-pixel units and double the result outside this shared routine.
10113               	; 	' Other actors retain pixel units and their existing movement rates.
10114               	; 	'
10115               	; 	' FIVE FRAMES, AND THREE WAS TOO FEW. At 2 px a frame five frames is 10 px,
10116               	; 	' and to skip a position window an actor must start outside it on one side
10117               	; 	' and land outside on the other, which needs 12. Three was the original bug
10118               	; 	' in miniature: the lift screen runs at almost exactly 20 passes a second,
10119               	; 	' which IS fdv = 3, so every hitch there lost a frame. The clamp exists for
10120               	; 	' a genuine stall and at five it only fires for one.
10121               	; pace_step:
10122               cvb_PACE_STEP

10625               	;
10626               	; 	' THE SIXTEENTH-PIXEL ACCUMULATOR. hx is one unsigned byte per screen
10627               	; 	' (2), so there is nowhere to keep a fraction -- the fraction lives here
10628               	; 	' and is spent as whole pixels. THREE IFs, not a loop and not a divide:
10629               	; 	' `%` and `/` both compile to a real TMS9900 DIV (CLAUDE.md 3A) and this
10630               	; 	' runs every pass.
10631               	; 	'
10632               	; 	' THE NUMBER OF DRAINS IS A CEILING ON THE SPEED, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE
10633               	; 	' POINT OF THIS COMMENT. Each IF can spend one whole pixel, so N drains
10634               	; 	' cap hspd at N px per pass NO MATTER WHAT hsp64 SAYS. The invariant is:
10635               	; 	'
10636               	; 	'     hacc is under 16 on entry, and hsp64 is at most 48,
10637               	; 	'     so hacc is under 64 here and three drains always suffice.
10638               	; 	'
10639               	; 	' KEEP hsp64 <= 48. This was quarter-pixels with TWO drains and the same
10640               	; 	' invariant written the same way -- "hsp4 is at most 8, so it can never
10641               	; 	' need a third" -- and it was correct until somebody set hsp4 = 9 without
10642               	; 	' re-reading it. The crook then ran at a flat 2.0 px/pass while every
10643               	; 	' comment, the design table and assets/checkchase.py all said 2.25, and
10644               	; 	' the surplus quarter leaked into hacc and wrapped the byte every 256
10645               	; 	' passes. Nothing failed; he simply arrived two thirds of a screen short
10646               	; 	' of his own escape. checkchase.py now counts these IFs and refuses a
10647               	; 	' speed the drains cannot deliver.
10648               	; 	'
10649               	; 	' 7, NOT 6, AND THE REASON IS MEASURED. Tracked off the reference video
10650               	; 	' (DESIGN.md 4a), the 2600's Kelly covers 0.40 screen widths a second and
10651               	; 	' its Harry 0.193 -- a ratio of 2.07. At hsp4 = 6 ours was 2.67, and the
10652               	; 	' crook visibly strolled. 7 brings it to 2.29. 8 would match the original
10653               	; 	' exactly and cannot be used: Kelly's route here is 1.95x Harry's, so a
10654               	; 	' speed ratio of 2.0 leaves the on-foot chase 0.2 s of slack, which is no
10655               	; 	' chase at all. checkchase.py holds the line.
10656               	; 	' STILL RUNNING FROM THE STAIRS -- and this has to come BEFORE the move,
10657               	; 	' not after it. It sat below the two `IF hmv` blocks, where all it could
10658               	; 	' still reach was the animation counter: he faced the right way, played

10756               	;
10757               	; 	' HE WALKS BY REAL TIME, NOT BY LOOP PASS -- one accumulate-and-drain per
10758               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAME rather than per pass. Everything that moves here used to be
10759               	; 	' per pass while the CLOCK is paced by the frame delta, so a busy screen
10760               	; 	' slowed Harry in real seconds and the clock did not slow with him: the
10761               	; 	' same uninterrupted escape finished with nine timer units in hand from a
10762               	; 	' light screen and none at all from the lift screen, decided by where the
10763               	; 	' player happened to be standing. Now he covers the same ground per second
10764               	; 	' wherever anybody is (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10765               	; 	'
10766               	; 	' A LOOP, NOT A MULTIPLY. `*` compiles to a real TMS9900 MPY, and reading a
10767               	; 	' 16-bit variable straight after one returns the product's HIGH word
10768               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). fdv is 1..3 here, so this is at most three adds.
10769               	; 	'
10770               	; 	' SIXTY-FOURTHS, AND ONLY TWO DRAINS -- both fall out of accumulating per
10771               	; 	' FRAME instead of per pass. He covers under a pixel a frame, so two drains
10772               	; 	' are ample where the per-pass version needed three; and the finer unit is
10773               	; 	' what makes the speed tunable at all. In sixteenths one step was about six
10774               	; 	' SECONDS of his route, so nothing landed near the buzzer; in sixty-fourths
10775               	; 	' it is about one and a half. Keep hsp64 <= 128: hacc is under 64 on entry,
10776               	; 	' so 64 + 128 stays inside a byte and two drains always suffice.
10777               	; 	'
10778               	; 	' AND THE STEP IS CLAMPED TO THREE FRAMES' WORTH, WHICH IS NOT A DETAIL.
10779               	; 	' Two tests sample his position once a pass and neither interpolates:
10780               	; 	'
10781               	; 	'   ARRIVAL   `hdx < 6` around the escalator or the roof door -- an ELEVEN
10782               	; 	'             pixel window. A step over 10 px can jump clean across it and
10783               	; 	'             he never arrives at all.
10784               	; 	'   THE CATCH `hdd < CATCHR` is 12, a 23-wide band, and Kelly closes 4 of
10785               	; 	'             it himself -- so Harry over ~18 px could pass through the Kop
10786               	; 	'             between two passes without either sample being inside it.
10787               	; 	'
10788               	; 	' The clamp and the drains live in pace_step now, with the reasoning; the
10789               	; 	' numbers above are what sized them. Measured: TIME 02 on the lift screen
10790               	; 	' against TIME 04 on a light one when the clamp was 3, and 00 against 09
10791               	; 	' before any of this.
10792               	; 	'
10793               	; 	' The ESCALATOR RIDE is deliberately untouched: it returns above this,
10794               	; 	' clocked one step per pass to stay locked to the moving staircase. A rider
10795               	; 	' advanced by the frame delta either drifts off the treads or makes the
10796               	; 	' steps run backwards (CLAUDE.md 3A, DESIGN.md 0f). It is about 3% of his
10797               	; 	' journey.
10798               	; 	'
10799               	; 	' `hanim` still advances by hspd and is still an ODOMETER -- pixels
10800               	; 	' travelled, not time -- so the run cycle stays locked to the ground at any
10801               	; 	' rate. A 9 px step moves it exactly one pose of its 8 px beat.

11262               	;
11263               	; 	' ======================================================================
11264               	; 	' COLLISIONS -- pure arithmetic against RAM, no VDP reads
11265               	; 	' ======================================================================
11266               	; 	' Kelly's box is [kfh, kfh + kh) above the slab; an obstacle's is
11267               	; 	' [ohb, oht). The ball's inset hitbox is what makes 8..10 avoidable both
11268               	; 	' ways -- without it there is a height at which the ball can be neither
11269               	; 	' jumped nor ducked, and an unavoidable hazard is not difficulty.
11270               	; 	' ONE HIT PER CONTACT, WITH A REFRACTORY PERIOD.
11271               	; 	'
11272               	; 	' The overlap test is true on every frame the player is touching
11273               	; 	' something, so with no latch at all one clumsy cart charges nine seconds
11274               	; 	' several times over -- and what the player sees is the clock jumping by
11275               	; 	' 27, from which the only available conclusion is that the penalty is
11276               	; 	' broken.
11277               	; 	'
11278               	; 	' A latch that clears on the first non-overlapping frame is still not
11279               	; 	' enough, and the case that breaks it is the BOUNCING BALL: it rises off
11280               	; 	' the player between bounces, which is a genuine loss of contact, so a
11281               	; 	' player standing still under one is taxed on every single bounce while
11282               	; 	' being given no opportunity to do anything about it. Technically two
11283               	; 	' collisions; in play, one situation.
11284               	; 	'
11285               	; 	' So obht() is a countdown, not a flag. A hit sets it to HITREF; it ticks
11286               	; 	' down only while the player is CLEAR, and the same obstacle cannot charge
11287               	; 	' again until it reaches zero. Contact holds the count up, so parking
11288               	; 	' inside something never earns a second penalty either.
11289               	; coll_obst:
11290               cvb_COLL_OBST

11753               	; 	' THE FLOOR CLEARS WHEN YOU ARE HIT, and stays clear until you re-enter
11754               	; 	' the screen. Nine seconds is a heavy penalty on a fifty-unit clock, and
11755               	; 	' taking it while still standing among the things that charged it -- with
11756               	; 	' a second hazard 48 px behind the first -- is how one mistake becomes
11757               	; 	' three. Clearing the row makes the penalty a single event you can walk
11758               	; 	' away from.
11759               	; 	'
11760               	; 	' BOTH SLOTS, WHATEVER IS IN THEM. Radios used to be exempt: they are
11761               	; 	' CHARACTERS stamped into the name table rather than sprites, so zeroing
11762               	; 	' the kind would have stopped them colliding while leaving them plainly
11763               	; 	' visible on the shelf, and a fixture that is still there has to still be
11764               	; 	' there. That was a reason to UNDRAW them, not a reason to keep them --
11765               	; 	' and it left the one hazard that cannot leave on its own as the only one
11766               	; 	' the mercy did not cover. haz_off now takes the characters with it.
11767               	; 	'
11768               	; 	' NOTHING RESTORES IT HERE. load_band repopulates the band from the
11769               	; 	' template, and it runs only on a seam crossing or a round start, so
11770               	; 	' "until the screen is re-entered" costs no state and no timer: leave and
11771               	; 	' come back and the hazards are simply placed again.
11772               	; 	'
11773               	; 	' THE CALL ITSELF IS IN THE MAIN LOOP, at the end of the freeze -- see
11774               	; 	' the hfz block there for why.
11775               	; 	' A HIT DOES NOT END A JUMP. This used to force ST_RUN and zero the arc,
11776               	; 	' which dropped him straight down out of mid-air onto whatever he happened
11777               	; 	' to be over -- and since the arc is ballistic and ignores the stick once
11778               	; 	' he is airborne (0l), that read as the game taking the controls away
11779               	; 	' rather than as a hit landing. The penalty is the nine units and the
11780               	; 	' hit sound; where he comes down is still his own arc.

11942               	; 	' AND THEY HAVE TO BE AT THE SAME HEIGHT, NOT MERELY ON THE SAME FLOOR.
11943               	; 	'
11944               	; 	' `hlv` does not change until a ride ENDS -- a crook stepping onto a
11945               	; 	' flight keeps the floor he left until he arrives at the next one. So
11946               	; 	' while he was most of a storey up or down the stairs he still counted as
11947               	; 	' standing on the floor he started from, and a Kop who ran over the head
11948               	; 	' of the flight arrested him through the floor. Reported from play:
11949               	; 	' "I run over top of him, even though we do not touch".
11950               	; 	'
11951               	; 	' It is the same shape of bug as the catch that fired at MAXIMUM
11952               	; 	' separation: a test that is right about one axis and silent about the
11953               	; 	' other, where the silent one happens to be true nearly all the time.
11954               	; 	'
11955               	; 	' UNSIGNED-SAFE. Riding up is above the shared floor and riding down is
11956               	; 	' below it, which is a signed quantity, and CVBasic's variables are not.
11957               	; 	' So both are collected as POSITIVE heights on opposite sides -- Kelly's
11958               	; 	' climb plus Harry's descent on one side, Harry's climb on the other --
11959               	; 	' and the difference is taken between two numbers that cannot go
11960               	; 	' negative. Two riders passing on the same flight measure the sum of
11961               	; 	' their heights, which is exactly the distance between them.

13144               	; 	' Rows 21-23, 16 chars wide, centred: 48 characters whose PATTERNS are
13145               	; 	' poked directly, so a moving dot costs two writes and no name-table

13147               	; 	' is at all -- he can be one pixel off-screen and completely invisible.
13148               	; 	'

13150               	; 	' is at base 4096 and no third-selection arithmetic is needed.
13151               	; 	'
13152               	; 	' BOTH DOTS ARE WHITE and Kelly's BLINKS. The manual wants Kelly black
13153               	; 	' and Harry white, but this is the TMS9918's two-colours-per-8x1-cell
13154               	; 	' mode: a black dot and a white dot on the same pixel row of the same
13155               	; 	' character cannot both exist. Blinking distinguishes them with one
13156               	; 	' colour, which is what RallyX does with its player dot.
13157               	; 	' THE STEPS MOVE, AND EVERY ESCALATOR ON SCREEN MOVES WITH THEM. A flight
13158               	; 	' is twelve characters -- six per direction, sliced out of a rendered
13159               	; 	' 64x40 bitmap by genart.py -- so rewriting those twelve PATTERNS animates
13160               	; 	' the lot: 96 bytes, no name-table traffic, and the same cost whether one
13161               	; 	' flight is visible or ten. The phases slide the cells ALONG the slope, so
13162               	; 	' the steps travel up the flight rather than drifting sideways.

13188               	; 	' ONE PHASE PER PASS, AND NEVER MORE. There are four phases covering an
13189               	; 	' 8 px period, so advancing by the frame delta ALIASES: at fdv 2 the
13190               	; 	' pattern flips between two positions half a period apart and the
13191               	; 	' direction stops being readable, and at fdv 3 the sequence runs 0,3,2,1
13192               	; 	' -- the staircase visibly runs BACKWARDS, carrying its steps down while
13193               	; 	' the rider goes up. That is the wagon-wheel effect, and no amount of
13194               	; 	' phase arithmetic fixes it: a 4-phase cycle can only be stepped by 1.
13195               	; 	'
13196               	; 	' So the ANIMATION is the clock here, and the rider is paced from it --
13197               	; 	' see move_kelly, which advances him by the same fixed 2-and-1 per pass
13198               	; 	' rather than by fdv. Locking the two together is the only way they
13199               	; 	' cannot drift, and it is what "the player moves at the rate the steps
13200               	; 	' carry him" actually means. The cost is that a ride takes 36 passes
13201               	; 	' rather than 36 frames, so it slows down when the loop does -- which is
13202               	; 	' the honest behaviour for a machine that is carrying you.
13203               	; 	escp = escp + 1

13216               	; 	#if NES
13217               	; 	' A VBLANK OF ITS OWN, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE-SCREEN FLASH.
13218               	; 	'
13219               	; 	' PPUBUF is not flushed when it is written -- it ACCUMULATES for the whole
13220               	; 	' pass and the NMI empties it in one go, so every VPOKE the radar makes,
13221               	; 	' every HUD digit and this upload all land in the SAME vblank. And the
13222               	; 	' handler's copy loop does not stop when vblank ends: it runs to the end of
13223               	; 	' the descriptor and then writes PPUADDR and both PPUSCROLLs, which
13224               	; 	' mid-frame re-points the PPU's own render address. The rest of that frame
13225               	; 	' is drawn from the wrong place. On screen that is not a dropped tile, it
13226               	; 	' is the ENTIRE PICTURE jumping for a frame -- which is what has been
13227               	; 	' reported, repeatedly, as the screen flashing on an escalator.
13228               	; 	'
13229               	; 	' The arithmetic says it cannot be anything else. NTSC vblank is about
13230               	; 	' 2273 CPU cycles; NMI entry, the flicker test and OAM DMA spend ~560 of
13231               	; 	' them before a single byte is copied. A copy descriptor costs ~50 cycles
13232               	; 	' plus 14 a byte, so these six characters -- 96 bytes, because a tile is
13233               	; 	' SIXTEEN bytes in two bitplanes, not eight -- are ~1400 on their own.
13234               	; 	' That leaves about 270 cycles, or SIX single-byte pokes, for everything
13235               	; 	' else the pass queued. The radar alone beats that whenever a dot moves.
13236               	; 	'
13237               	; 	' Nothing smaller fixes it, because the overrun is per FRAME, not per
13238               	; 	' second: slowing the animation down just makes the bad frames rarer.
13239               	; 	' Splitting the six characters across two frames tears the staircase, and
13240               	; 	' only three of the six have a constant second bitplane, so dropping a
13241               	; 	' plane does not buy a frame's worth either. What DOES work is giving the
13242               	; 	' upload a vblank with nothing else in it: this WAIT flushes the pass's
13243               	; 	' radar and HUD writes, and the descriptor queued below is then almost all
13244               	; 	' the next vblank has to carry -- ~1960 cycles of 2273, inside the window
13245               	; 	' with room to spare.
13246               	; 	'
13247               	; 	' IT COSTS ONE FRAME A PASS, on the two screens that carry a flight and
13248               	; 	' nowhere else -- esc_tick has already returned on the other six. The
13249               	; 	' rider is paced from the animation rather than from the frame delta (see
13250               	; 	' below), so a slower pass slows the ride too and the two cannot drift.
13251               	; 	WAIT
13252               	; 	#endif
13253               	; 	' ONLY THE CELLS THAT MOVE, AND ONLY THIS SCREEN'S. genart.py measures
13254               	; 	' which cells move -- the step cells and the COMPOSITE copies of them
13255               	; 	' that cross a floor -- and groups them WEST then EAST, because only one
13256               	; 	' direction is ever on screen: screen 0 carries a west flight and screen
13257               	; 	' 7 an east one.
13258               	; 	'
13259               	; 	' THIS IS THE ONLY PER-PASS WORK UNIQUE TO THESE TWO SCREENS, and it is
13260               	; 	' `define_char`, which in bitmap mode is LDIRVM3 -- the TRIPLE copy, once
13261               	; 	' per screen third. It therefore costs three times what the character
13262               	; 	' count suggests, which is why these screens run slower than the rest.
13263               	; 	'
13264               	; 	' THE WEST SCREEN USED TO COST HALF AS MUCH AGAIN, because it carries TWO
13265               	; 	' flights: floor 1's crosses into a shop floor and floor 3's into the
13266               	; 	' roof, so it needed both composite sets -- nine characters against the
13267               	; 	' east's six, 216 bytes a pass against 144. It measured 20 passes a
13268               	; 	' second where the east screen managed 24-26. The two sets are
13269               	; 	' PIXEL-IDENTICAL and are never wanted in the same screen THIRD, so they
13270               	; 	' share their characters now and are told apart by the per-third colour
13271               	; 	' table (see esc_deck_col in setup). Six either side.
13272               	; 	'
13273               	; 	' The handrail and the frame sit past the end of both ranges and never
13274               	; 	' move at all.
13275               	; 	IF klsc = 0 THEN

13901               	; 	' A LEVEL BAND IS SIX PIXEL ROWS ON THE NES AND FOUR ON THE TI.
13902               	; 	'
13903               	; 	' It was six everywhere once. It shrank to four to buy eight empty pixel
13904               	; 	' rows -- four above the instrument and four below -- so the scanner did
13905               	; 	' not butt against the shop floor above it and the bottom of the screen.
13906               	; 	'
13907               	; 	' On the NES that margin now comes from somewhere else: the name table is
13908               	; 	' thirty rows to the TI's twenty-four, so the strip runs past the canvas to
13909               	; 	' the bottom edge and the grey either side of the instrument is real cells
13910               	; 	' rather than blank rows inside it. That gives the band its two rows back,
13911               	; 	' and the instrument goes from 16 pixels tall to 24 -- half again, which is
13912               	; 	' what "not quite so vertically thin" asks for.
13913               	; 	'
13914               	; 	' The TI cannot follow: its name table ENDS at row 23, the scanner is on
13915               	; 	' the last three rows, and there is nowhere to put the margin. So the band
13916               	; 	' height is per-target and every row offset below is derived from it.

13947               	;
13948               	; scan_or1:
13949               cvb_SCAN_OR1
13950               	; 	' THE ONE READ-MODIFY-WRITE ON THE PATTERN TABLE. The radar ORs a
13951               	; 	' pixel row into a canvas character, so it has to know what is already
13952               	; 	' there. On the NES that read comes from nsc, which scan_wipe zeroed
13953               	; 	' and which only this routine writes -- so it is exact, not an
13954               	; 	' approximation of what the PPU holds.
13955               	; 	' AND ON THE NES IT CLEARS RATHER THAN SETS, WHICH IS NOT A TYPO.
13956               	; 	'
13957               	; 	' This routine only ever draws the escalator flights (three call sites,
13958               	; 	' all in scan_escs). On the TI they are drawn as INK and coloured black by
13959               	; 	' scan_escc, so the bits go IN. Here the canvas is wiped to green -- plane
13960               	; 	' 0 set everywhere, see scan_wipe. Black is index 2: clear plane 0 and
13961               	; 	' set plane 1 for the same pixels. Preserve the caller's pattern address.
13962               	; 	'
13963               	; 	' 255 - fm1 is NOT fm1: a byte subtracted from all-ones never borrows, so
13964               	; 	' it is the bitwise complement without needing one.
13965               	; 	#if NES
13966               	; 	#nsi = #sda - #nsb
13967               	; 	sva = nsc(#nsi)
13968               	; 	fmn = 255 - fm1
13969               	; 	sva = sva AND fmn
13970               	; 	nsc(#nsi) = sva
13971               	; 	VPOKE #sda,sva
13972               	; 	#nsi = #nsi + 8
13973               	; 	sva = nsc(#nsi)
13974               	; 	sva = sva OR fm1
13975               	; 	nsc(#nsi) = sva

14074               	;
14075               	; 	' Blank the canvas by WRITING zeros rather than copying 384 of them out
14076               	; 	' of ROM. This runs twice a game -- at setup and on a new Krook -- so a
14077               	; 	' loop costs nothing anybody can perceive, and it hands the fixed area
14078               	; 	' back the best part of half a kilobyte, which is the budget that
14079               	; 	' actually binds. Paced in bursts: a few hundred VDP writes in a single
14080               	; 	' frame are silently dropped (CLAUDE.md 3A).
14081               	; scan_wipe:
14082               cvb_SCAN_WIPE
14083               	; 	' THIS ADDRESS IS A CHARACTER CODE IN DISGUISE, AND IT WENT STALE.
14084               	; 	' 4096 is the pattern table's BOTTOM THIRD -- rows 16-23, which is
14085               	; 	' band 0 and the radar together -- and the canvas characters begin at
14086               	; 	' genart's SCAN_FIRST, so the base is 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8. It was
14087               	; 	' written out by hand as 4096 + 160*8 when SCAN_FIRST was 160; art
14088               	; 	' added later moved SCAN_FIRST to 208 and nothing moved this with it,
14089               	; 	' so the wipe zeroed the 48 characters BELOW the canvas and never
14090               	; 	' touched the canvas at all.
14091               	; 	'
14092               	; 	' Two of those forty-eight are STRUCTURE. ENDWALL is the building's
14093               	; 	' outside wall and SLABP is a pillar's cap. Blanking a pattern in ONE
14094               	; 	' THIRD leaves a character that draws correctly everywhere else and
14095               	; 	' falls back to its own background colour here -- so the GROUND FLOOR's
14096               	; 	' outside wall turned into plain green while the identical wall one
14097               	; 	' storey up was perfect, and the ground floor's pillars lost the brick
14098               	; 	' carried up through the bar above them. ENDWALL appears only on
14099               	; 	' screens 0 and 7, which is exactly why it was reported as happening
14100               	; 	' only on the escalator screens, mirrored side to side.
14101               	; 	'
14102               	; 	' The name table was correct the whole time. Probing it said so, four
14103               	; 	' times. It was the GLYPH that was empty, in one third only -- which a
14104               	; 	' probe that copies the character somewhere else to look at it cannot
14105               	; 	' see, because the copy renders from a different third's pattern.
14106               	; 	'
14107               	; 	' renumber.py rewrites this line from genart.SCAN_FIRST, and
14108               	; 	' checkstruct.py fails the build if the two disagree.

14779               	; #if NES
14780               	; 	' ----------------------------------------------------------------------
14781               	; 	' Attributes select a palette per 16x16 quadrant. gennescolor.py derives
14782               	; 	' eight screen tables; draw_screen stages one in nesb, masks fixtures,
14783               	; 	' then uploads all 64 bytes through nes_attrs_put within one vblank.
14784               	; 	' A MESSAGE BOX GOES GOLD ON DARK BLUE, and the caller says which four
14785               	; 	' bytes in #nav.
14786               	; 	'
14787               	; 	' The text's paper is index 1 and its ink index 3 (see the font upload);
14788               	; 	' over the store those are P0's green and gold -- the same green the box is
14789               	; 	' sitting on, which is what made the messages hard to read. P1 is the HUD's
14790               	; 	' palette, dark blue and gold, so pointing the box's attribute bytes at it
14791               	; 	' gives a message the same treatment as the score line.
14792               	; 	'
14793               	; 	' FOUR BYTES AND NOT ONE MORE. An attribute byte covers four characters by
14794               	; 	' four, and the box is sized and placed to cover exactly four of them
14795               	; 	' (gentitle.py BOX_ROW/BOX_COL/BOX_W): byte columns 2..5, which is name
14796               	; 	' columns 8..23. Anything wider would recolour shop floor beside the box.
14797               	; 	'
14798               	; 	' THIS IS A ROUTINE BECAUSE IT WAS WRITTEN OUT TWICE AND MISSED A THIRD
14799               	; 	' TIME. GOT HIM! kept the store's colours while the other boxes changed,
14800               	; 	' and nothing failed -- it is a readable message in the wrong palette.
14801               	; 	' checkmsg.py now fails the build if a message box is drawn without one of
14802               	; 	' these beside it.
14803               	; 	'
14804               	; 	' Nothing puts them back, because nothing needs to: every path out of a
14805               	; 	' message box redraws the screen, and draw_screen calls nes_attr, which
14806               	; 	' rewrites all sixty-four.
14807               	; nes_boxatt:
14808               	; 	WAIT
14809               	; 	' Top half: P1 text. Bottom half: P3, whose navy matches P1 paper.
14810               	; 	' Only the third row is painted navy; leave the fourth row's tiles alone.
14811               	; 	#nsrc = 8776
14812               	; 	IF #nav = 9178 THEN #nsrc = 8648
14813               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 3
14814               	; 		VPOKE #nav,245
14815               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1
14816               	; 	NEXT nai
14817               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 15

14824               	; nes_attr:

14826               	; 	' escalator or marquee CHR uploads. One 64-byte copy fits one vblank.

15307               	;
15308               	; 	' THE BONUS IS COUNTED OUT, NOT AWARDED. Dropping the whole sum into the
15309               	; 	' score in one frame tells the player a number; ticking the clock down a
15310               	; 	' unit at a time, with the score climbing and a beat under each step,
15311               	; 	' tells them what the number was FOR. It is the pay-off for every second
15312               	; 	' they saved, and every arcade game of this era spends a moment on it.
15313               	; 	'
15314               	; 	' It also costs nothing to get right: the loop already has to run down
15315               	; 	' `tsec`, so the animation IS the calculation, and the repeated-addition
15316               	; 	' note below stops applying -- each step adds one band's worth.
15317               	; 	'
15318               	; 	' x100 for Krooks 1-9, x200 for 10-15, x300 from 16. Two independent
15319               	; 	' sources agree on those bands; the manual's own wording suggests
15320               	; 	' 1-8 / 9-16 / 17+ and DESIGN.md 0 records the disagreement.
15321               	; 	'
15322               	; 	' IN UNITS OF TEN, WHICH IS WHAT THE SCORE IS COUNTED IN, so the bands are
15323               	; 	' 10 / 20 / 30 and not 100 / 200 / 300.
15324               	; 	'
15325               	; 	' They were 100 / 200 / 300 and paid TEN TIMES the right bonus -- 1,000 a
15326               	; 	' time unit where the original pays 100. `add_score` takes `#addv` in units
15327               	; 	' of ten (the prize beside it is `#addv = 5` for fifty points, and the bonus
15328               	; 	' Kop threshold is `#nextk = 1000` for ten thousand), so writing the band in
15329               	; 	' POINTS here shifted every tally one decimal place. Reported from play as
15330               	; 	' "it seems like you awarded 1000 per time unit left" -- exactly right.
15331               	; 	'
15332               	; 	' Nothing failed: 1,000 a unit is a plausible-looking number, the digits
15333               	; 	' all line up, and the only symptom is a score that runs away. The tell is
15334               	; 	' a constant written in a different unit from the routine it is passed to,
15335               	; 	' which is the same class of fault as the px-per-pass speeds in 3A.
15336               	; 	'
15337               	; 	' (This is also why the old comment here said "#bval MUST BE 16-BIT: 300
15338               	; 	' does not fit in a byte". At 10 / 20 / 30 it would, but it stays 16-bit
15339               	; 	' because `#addv` is, and a byte here would buy two bytes of ROM in
15340               	; 	' exchange for a truncation trap the next time somebody edits a band.)
15341               	; bonus_count:
15342               cvb_BONUS_COUNT

15484               	;
15485               	; 	' AND IT ENDS ON ITS LAST BLIP -- there is no closing accent.
15486               	; 	'
15487               	; 	' Two were tried. The bench's own ending for this variant rose a fourth,
15488               	; 	' to 2,542 Hz, and a square wave there is a shriek -- the same fault the
15489               	; 	' pickup was rewritten for. Dropping it an OCTAVE BELOW the ticks, to
15490               	; 	' 518 Hz, was reported the same way, and that one cannot be too high by
15491               	; 	' any measure: it is the lowest note in the effect.
15492               	; 	'
15493               	; 	' So the complaint is not the pitch, it is the extra note. A tally is
15494               	; 	' arithmetic, and arithmetic finishes when the last term is added; a
15495               	; 	' flourish after it is a second event the player has to interpret, and
15496               	; 	' the HUD has already said the clock is empty. The count stops when the
15497               	; 	' counting stops.

15856               	;
15857               	; 	' A SOUND STILL PLAYING WHEN THE ROUND ENDS IS ALLOWED TO FINISH.
15858               	; 	'
15859               	; 	' This used to open with a bare `GOSUB snd_off`, which cut it dead. That
15860               	; 	' was not an accident: the decay counters are ticked by the MAIN LOOP, and
15861               	; 	' this pause REPLACES the main loop, so a tone left latched with nothing
15862               	; 	' ticking it hangs for the full ninety frames -- the sticky-audio failure
15863               	; 	' this game has already shipped twice. The answer is to DRAIN the counters
15864               	; 	' rather than to stop silencing.
15865               	; 	'
15866               	; 	' CLEAR THE PENDING LATCHES FIRST. sf* flags are sounds that have not
15867               	; 	' happened yet; left set, the drain below would START one and the pause
15868               	; 	' would end with a fresh note ringing into the next round.
15869               	; 	'
15870               	; 	' THEN TICK sfx_tick WHOLE, not some decay-only part of it. The five
15871               	; 	' counters do not all live in one place: sot, sht and spt are a block at
15872               	; 	' the tail, but spz (the prize arpeggio) and swt (the jump warble) tick up
15873               	; 	' among the code that starts sounds. Draining only the tail would finish a
15874               	; 	' footstep and still cut the arpeggio, which is the one effect with a
15875               	; 	' phrase worth saving. Calling the whole routine also leaves the write
15876               	; 	' order on CHANNEL 2 alone, which spz and spt share.
15877               	; 	'
15878               	; 	' EVERY THIRD FRAME, because the main loop runs about 2.5 frames per pass
15879               	; 	' and this loop waits one frame per turn. Ticking every frame would play
15880               	; 	' everything at two and a half times its tuned speed. Three frames a tick
15881               	; 	' is ~17% slow and gives 30 ticks against the longest effect's 20 passes.
15882               	; 	'
15883               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNTS TICKS, NOT FRAMES, which is what makes the pacing free.
15884               	; 	' Counting 91 frames and firing on every third needs a second counter, an
15885               	; 	' increment and a test -- 48 bytes, on a fixed area with 66 left. Counting
15886               	; 	' 31 TICKS of three WAITs each is the same 93 frames and the same three
15887               	; 	' frames per tick, with none of that. The duration changes by two frames.
15888               	; 	'
15889               	; 	' snd_off still runs at the END, as the backstop for anything the drain
15890               	; 	' did not finish.
15891               	; pause_beat:

15899               	; 	' call sites would have cost code to say the same thing worse.
15900               	; 	'
15901               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNT AND NOT THE WAITS. sfx_tick runs once per pass, so it

16323               	;
16324               	; 	' THE LOW-TIME WARNING IS SILENT. There was a beep a second under ten, and
16325               	; 	' it was the wrong instrument for the job: the last ten seconds are the
16326               	; 	' busiest part of a round, so a repeating tone arrives exactly when the
16327               	; 	' player most needs to hear the hazards, and it fought the prize arpeggio
16328               	; 	' for channel 2 as well. The flash says the same thing and says it in the
16329               	; 	' place the player is already looking.
16330               	;
16331               	; 	' FOOTSTEPS ARE NOISE, AND ON THE NOISE CHANNEL -- testsounds variant A.
16332               	; 	'
16333               	; 	' They were two alternating TONES on channel 0, which is neither what the
16334               	; 	' original does nor a good use of a channel: the recording says a footstep
16335               	; 	' is a short burst of white noise, and channel 3 was sitting unused while
16336               	; 	' the footsteps and the jump sweep shared channel 0 and had to take turns.
16337               	; 	'
16338               	; 	' TESTSOUNDS RUN D: a SHORT tick at the measured RATE.
16339               	; 	'
16340               	; 	' The two dials are independent and both were tried at the bench. The
16341               	; 	' 2600 plays a 64 ms burst every 165 ms -- six a second -- and variant A
16342               	; 	' copies both. Ten a second was tried on the way here and reads as
16343               	; 	' hurrying rather than running. What D changes is not the cadence but the
16344               	; 	' TICK: two frames rather than four, and a notch louder to carry at half
16345               	; 	' the length. Same six a second, less of it.
16346               	; 	'
16347               	; 	' EIGHT A SECOND, AND THE ACCUMULATOR NOW CARRIES ITS REMAINDER.
16348               	; 	'
16349               	; 	' sfw counted pixels and the trigger did `sfw = 0`, THROWING AWAY whatever
16350               	; 	' was past the threshold. kspd is about four pixels a pass, so a threshold
16351               	; 	' of 17 did not fire at 17 -- it fired at the first multiple past it, about
16352               	; 	' 20, and every rate this was ever set to came out slower than the number
16353               	; 	' said: the "six a second" was 5.2 and the "ten" that read as hurrying was
16354               	; 	' really 8.7. Subtracting the threshold instead keeps the fraction, so the
16355               	; 	' rate is what it claims to be at any walking speed.
16356               	; 	'
16357               	; 	' MEASURED OFF THE COLECOVISION: 14 px, about 7.4 a second.
16358               	; 	'
16359               	; 	' It was 15 px and 6.9 a second, picked between an 8.0 that read as
16360               	; 	' slightly hurried and a 6.1 that read as trudging -- a judgement between
16361               	; 	' two other judgements, with nothing underneath it. The ColecoVision
16362               	; 	' recording settles it: footfalls land every 0.130 s across a twelve-second
16363               	; 	' continuous run, which is 7.7 a second, and that is the one finding in the
16364               	; 	' whole sound analysis the method resolves EXACTLY -- a rhythm rather than a
16365               	; 	' pitch, counted off the RMS track rather than inferred from a spectrum.
16366               	; 	' (colecosounds variant 1A; assets/sfx/sfxref-coleco.md has the working.)
16367               	; 	'
16368               	; 	' 104 px/s over 14 px is 7.43 a second. 13 px would give 8.00, and 7.7 sits
16369               	; 	' almost exactly between them -- so this is the nearer of the two, and it is
16370               	; 	' also the one that does not walk back into the 8.0 that was rejected by ear.
16371               	; 	'
16372               	; 	' WHY THE GAME KEEPS A DISTANCE AND THE BENCH KEEPS A CADENCE. The bench
16373               	; 	' plays a fixed eight frames between steps because it has no walking to tie
16374               	; 	' them to; the game accumulates PIXELS TRAVELLED, so the feet keep time with
16375               	; 	' the legs when he is slowed or stopped. Matching "7.4 a second" therefore
16376               	; 	' means matching it AT HIS WALKING SPEED, and assumes the ColecoVision's
16377               	; 	' crook walks at ours -- which the recording cannot confirm.
16378               	; 	'
16379               	; 	' The dial is this one constant and the subtraction below, which must stay
16380               	; 	' threshold + 1 or the carry is wrong.
16381               	; 	'
16382               	; 	' SOT = 2 IS THE SHORTEST TICK THERE IS, and 1 is SILENCE. The decay block

16386               	; 	' sound -- about 42 ms against the bench's 33, as close as a per-pass timer

16389               	; 	' Register 4 is white noise at the fastest rate.

16722               	;
16723               	; 	' EVERYTHING BELOW THIS LINE IS ASSEMBLED INTO BANK 1, so the INCLUDE order
16724               	; 	' is load-bearing and nothing but data may follow it.
16725               	; 	'
16726               	; 	' THE FONT IS NOW IN THE BANK TOO, and it used to be deliberately outside:
16727               	; 	' keeping one readable thing in bank 0 means a bank-selection mistake shows
16728               	; 	' as "text survives, art does not" rather than a uniformly blank screen,
16729               	; 	' which is a genuinely useful thing to have when a bank goes wrong.
16730               	; 	'
16731               	; 	' THE FONT HAS A BANK OF ITS OWN, and the reason is not its size.
16732               	; 	'
16733               	; 	' Bank 1 was FULL -- six spare bytes of 8,192 -- which shut the door on
16734               	; 	' moving anything else out of the fixed area, and the fixed area is the
16735               	; 	' only budget that cannot be grown (linkticart writes exactly three
16736               	; 	' loader pages and discards the rest; they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
16737               	; 	' >A000, not cart ROM). A second bank costs a bigger cart -- five pages
16738               	; 	' round up to eight, so 32 KB becomes 64 KB -- and buys back the ability
16739               	; 	' to keep evacuating data out of code.
16740               	; 	'
16741               	; 	' THE FONT IS THE RIGHT TENANT because it is read ONCE. Two DEFINEs copy
16742               	; 	' it into VRAM at setup and nothing looks at it again, so it is the only
16743               	; 	' block here that can sit on a page which is not permanently mapped. See
16744               	; 	' setup_font: bank 2 is selected for those two statements and bank 1 for
16745               	; 	' the whole of the rest of the program.
16746               	; 	'
16747               	; 	' EVERYTHING ELSE STAYS IN BANK 1, because everything else is read during
16748               	; 	' play -- art on a screen crossing, templates on a band blit, the lookup
16749               	; 	' tables every pass. One permanently-mapped bank for all of it means
16750               	; 	' there is no switch to miss.
16751               	; 	#if TI994A
16752               	; 	BANK 2
16753      07E6     BANK_0_FREE:	EQU >fffe-$
     **** ****     > .rept

16892               	; 	' THE COLOUR TABLE, 472 bytes of the same value ($B4 = light yellow ink on dark blue).
16893               	; 	'
16894               	; 	' Loaded with DEFINE COLOR 32,59,font_col, which is ONE synchronous call that
16895               	; 	' writes all three screen thirds (define_color always does the LDIRVM3 triple

16898               	; 	' screen used to fill in visibly rather than appearing at once.

16901               	; 	' whatever follows in ROM as colour data, with no error at build or run time.

17037               	; 	' LIVES IN BANK 2 -- read once by those DEFINEs.

17657               	; 	' Keystone Kapers art -- GENERATED by assets/genart.py. Do not edit; regenerate.
17658               	; 	'
17659               	; 	' EVERY SPRITE IS 16x16: sprite size and magnification are GLOBAL on the
17660               	; 	' TMS9918, so small objects are drawn small INSIDE a 16x16 box rather than
17661               	; 	' being small sprites.

17665               	; 	' floor is at y = FLOORY - 16.
17666               	; 	'

17668               	; 	' the right. Every block is an EVEN number of bytes -- an odd DATA BYTE run
17669               	; 	' silently misaligns every word table after it (CLAUDE.md 3A).

18785               	;
18786               	; 	' -------------------------------------------------- scanner canvas
18787               	; 	' Chars 208-255: 16 cols x 3 rows over screen rows 21-23. Blank to start;
18788               	; 	' dots are plotted by VPOKEing the PATTERN table (rows 21-23 sit in the
18789               	; 	' third screen third, so every scanner pattern is at base 4096).
18790               	;
18791               	; 	' --------------------------------------------------- font colours
18792               	; 	' Chars 32-90, EIGHT bytes each. Without this the font keeps whatever
18793               	; 	' CVBasic left in the colour table, which on a green store made the HUD
18794               	; 	' unreadable.
18795               	;
18796               	; esc_deck:	' 6 x (char, 8 colour bytes) -- write into the THIRD-0 colour table at 8192 + char*8, once, at setup
18797               cvb_ESC_DECK

     718E 1B1A     
     7190 1A1A     
     7192 1C1C

18903               	; 	INCLUDE "store.bas"
18904               	; 	' Keystone Kapers store -- GENERATED by assets/genstore.py. Do not edit.
18905               	; 	'
18906               	; 	' EIGHT band templates of 5 rows x 32 cols (160 bytes each) plus a 32-byte
18907               	; 	' index over (level, screen). The whole 8-screen, 4-level building is about
18908               	; 	' 1.3 KB instead of the 5,120 bytes it would cost to store literally.
18909               	; 	'
18910               	; 	' All eight templates are ONE contiguous block under ONE label, so a band
18911               	; 	' blit is
18912               	; 	'     SCREEN stor_tpl, tpl*160, toprow*32, 32, 5, 32
18913               	; 	' with no label ladder -- SCREEN needs a literal label and a label cannot be
18914               	; 	' chosen by a variable, which is why RallyX needed a 4-way IF over its maze
18915               	; 	' tables. One block sidesteps it.
18916               	; 	'
18917               	; 	' 160 is EVEN, so this cannot leave the location counter odd and misalign
18918               	; 	' the word tables defined after it.
18919               	; 	'
18920               	; 	' template ids:
18921               	; 	'   0 T_AISLE_A
18922               	; 	'   1 T_AISLE_B
18923               	; 	'   2 T_ESC_W
18924               	; 	'   3 T_ESC_E
18925               	; 	'   4 T_ELEV
18926               	; 	'   5 T_ROOF0
18927               	; 	'   6 T_ROOF1
18928               	; 	'   7 T_ROOF2
18929               	; 	'   8 T_ROOF3
18930               	; 	'   9 T_ROOF4
18931               	; 	'   10 T_ROOF5
18932               	; 	'   11 T_ROOF6
18933               	; 	'   12 T_ROOF7
18934               	; 	'   13 T_END_W
18935               	; 	'   14 T_END_E
18936               	;
18937               	; stor_tpl:	' 15 templates x 160 bytes

19553               	;
19554               	; 	' THE SKYLINE'S LAST BAND WITHOUT ITS YELLOW, high nibble ink, low nibble
19555               	; 	' paper, one byte a scan line -- the same shape genart emits into
19556               	; 	' store_col. SKY2 is white-on-9 throughout instead of turning to paper 10
19557               	; 	' at row 4; BLDGL holds its blue one row longer and then meets its own
19558               	; 	' grey wall. Both are the generated bytes with 10 replaced by 9 and
19559               	; 	' nothing else changed. See setup_rest.
19560               	; #if NES
19561               	; nes_sky2c:
19562               	; 	DATA BYTE $F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9
19563               	; nes_bldlc:
19564               	; 	DATA BYTE $B9,$B9,$B9,$B9,$B9,$BE,$BE,$BE
19565               	; #endif
19566               	;
19567               	; 	' THE IN-GAME FONT'S COLOUR, one byte a scan line and eight a character for
19568               	; 	' all 59 of them. $B4 is light yellow on dark blue -- ink index 3, paper index 1 --
19569               	; 	' and which colours those are is then the attribute table's business, per
19570               	; 	' region: dark blue behind the HUD, the store's green behind a message box.
19571               	; 	'
19572               	; 	' 472 bytes of one repeated value. That reads like waste and is the cheap
19573               	; 	' option: ROM is three budgets here and this is not the scarce one, while
19574               	; 	' the alternative is a second font (impossible -- only eleven free codes)
19575               	; 	' or a new uploader parameter (no RAM -- two bytes left).

19577               	; nes_fcol:
